Response:
Thank you for your thorough review and constructive comments. We have
carefully revised the manuscript according to your comments. The replies to
each of your concern are listed below.
Point 1:
Why was liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) chosen as the thermoelectric matrix
instead of materials like hydrogels? As one of the most common smart materials,
this paper fails to highlight LCE's stimulus responsiveness or shape-
programming capabilities.
Response: Special thanks to you for raising this issue. This manuscript selects
LCE as the ionic thermoelectric matrix instead of other hydrogels primarily to
address the current challenges and limitations in the ionic thermoelectric field,
including electrolyte leakage, insufficient mechanical properties, and singular
optimization strategies. The design rationale for using LCE as the
thermoelectric matrix is as follows:
(1) Ionic thermoelectric materials based on hydrogels often require high-loading
of ionic electrolytes and the addition of multi-component ionic donors to achieve
high performance, leading to issues such as liquid leakage and difficulties in
encapsulation, which limit their practical applications (Sci. Adv. 9, eadk2098
(2023); Nat. Com. (2019)10:1093). In contrast, our work utilizes LCE as the
matrix and employs a solution immersion method to impart thermoelectric
properties. By leveraging the structural advantages of m-LCE network that
enable enlarged mobility differences between anions and cations without
requiring additional ionic donors, effectively preventing ionic liquid leakage..
Moreover, thanks to the hydrophobic nature and highly crosslinked network
structure of LCE, the material significantly reduces sensitivity to external
humidity (Adv. Funct. Mater.2013,23,3070-3076), avoiding interference with
thermoelectric performance. As a result, LCE i-TE materials can operate at
room temperature without encapsulation;
(2) Most current high-performance ionic thermoelectric materials require
precise regulate and optimization of their network structures, often resulting in
molecular chains that cannot withstand significant stress, leading to poor
mechanical properties-typically with stress and strain levels hardly exceeding
2022, 15, 2049-2060). This inevitably creates a trade-off between mechanical
and thermoelectric performance. In this study, the LCE i-TE fibers inherit the
excellent intrinsic mechanical properties of LCE, enabling them to exhibit both
notable thermoelectric characteristics and robust mechanical behavior. This
successfully addresses the mechanical limitations of existing ionic
thermoelectric materials and enhances their potential for applications in
wearable devices and actuators fields;
(3) Current strategies for improving the performance of ionic thermoelectric
materials often rely on regulating interactions between ions and polymer
matrices, incorporating multicomponent doping, or controlling external
conditions such as relative humidity and pH, such as reported in Nature
Communications (2022) 13:221; Adv. Mater. 2024, 36, 2402386; Energy
Environ. Sci., 2022, 15, 2049-2060. These approaches generally involve
complex preparation processes and stringent testing conditions, resulting in
poor reproducibility of material performance, phase separation, and insufficient
structural and performance stability, which limit the practical applicability of ionic
thermoelectric materials. In this work, the use of LCE as a matrix leverages its
programmable molecular chain structure to achieve a highly ordered
arrangement, which facilitates thermal-driven ion migration within the system.
This structural optimization intrinsically enhances the thermoelectric
performance of the material, offering a more practical and scalable pathway for
advanced applications.
Furthermore, as a common smart material, LCE exhibits excellent stimulus
responsiveness and shape-programming capabilities, making it widely
applicable in actuators, artificial muscles, and other fields. Similar to the smart
LCE i-TE fibers reported in our previous work (Nature
Communications,2025,16:5445), which demonstrated integrated actuation and
sensing capabilities under thermal stimulation, the m-LCE i-TE fibers in this
manuscript also exhibit thermo-actuating behavior. As shown in Figure S41, at
different temperatures, the LCE i-TE fiber undergoes transverse contraction
macroscopically due to the changes in the orientation of mesogens under high
temperature. At 70 °C, the contraction rate reached 18.6%, and the fiber
gradually returned to its original length as the temperature decreased. DSC
measurements of the LCE i-TE fiber revealed a glass transition temperature of
42.1 °C and a clear point at 90.6 °C, indicating a liquid crystalline phase
temperature range of 42.1-90.6 °C (Figure S42). This suggests that deformation
can occur when the temperature exceeds 42.1 °C. However, the LCE i-TE fiber
presented in this study is primarily designed for sensing applications in
wearable thermal energy scenarios. As demonstrated in Figures 5(i-k) and
Supplementary Figure S40, the voltage signal response under varying
temperature differences between the human body and the environment is used
for information feedback. Since the contacted heat sources in this work do not
reach the thermal actuation range of the material, no thermally induced
deformation occurs.

Response: We sincerely appreciate your valuable suggestions. We apologize
for the oversight in not including the fabrication method of side-chain liquid
crystal elastomer (s-LCE) i-TE fibers in the manuscript. The preparation of s-
LCE i-TE fibers follows the procedure reported in the literature (Nature
Communications; (2025) 16:5445), utilizing RM257 as the liquid crystal
mesogen, EDDET and PETMP as the soft segment and crosslinker,
respectively, and DPA as the catalyst. Briefly, 2.4 g RM257, 0.7 g EDDET, and
0.1 g PETMP were dissolved in 2.4 mL ethyl acetate and stirred at 70°C for 1
h. Then, 9 μL DPA was added, and the mixture was stirred for 1 min to obtain
the LCE precursor solution. The solution was subsequently injected into a
polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) tube (inner diameter: 2 mm) via syringe and
cured horizontally at room temperature for 12 h. The resulting s-LCE fiber was
then peeled from the tube. The s-LCE i-TE fibers were prepared by immersing
the s-LCE fibers in an ionic liquid solution for a designated duration using the
solution impregnation method. This fabrication procedure has now been added
to the materials preparation section of the manuscript.
The conclusion that “the mesogens only one terminal connects to the
molecular backbone” is primarily supported by Nuclear Magnetic Resonance
(NMR) characterization of the material. For s-LCE: 1H NMR (CDCl₃, δ, ppm):
6.25-5.68 (d, 4H, CH₂=CH-); 5.99 (m, 2H, CH₂=CH-); 1.36 (m, 4H, -CH₂). As
shown in Figure 2(b), the 1H NMR spectrum of s-LCE i-TE fibers displays a
peak area ratio of olefinic protons to methylene protons of 1:1.59, which is
consistent with the single-end olefin structure (Polymer 52 (2011) 5075-5084).
This indicates that the material contains fewer olefinic protons with only one
terminal olefin group connected to the molecular backbone, providing direct
evidence for the side-chain LCE structure.

Response: We sincerely appreciate your valuable feedback. We indeed
omitted the explanation of this part in the manuscript. The reason for not
selecting RM82 for the synthesis of side-chain LCE fibers in this study is
primarily due to differences in the thermoelectric properties of the LCE fiber
prepared from various liquid crystal mesogen. Specifically, in terms of molecular
chain structure, RM82 contains six methylene groups, while RM257 has only
three. This structural difference results in a softer network formed by RM82
compared to that of RM257. Given the significant differences in synthesis
processes between main-chain and side-chain LCE fiber, if RM82 were directly
used to synthesize LCE fibers for ionic thermoelectric materials, the increased
viscosity of the material system would hinder ion migration and thus adversely
affect the ionic thermoelectric performance. To verify this, we employed the
synthesis process for s-LCE i-TE fibers using RM82 as the liquid crystal
mesogen, as shown in the figure below. Furthermore, using the impregnation
method described in this work, we compared the thermopower of s-LCE i-TE
fibers synthesized with RM82 and RM257 after impregnation with LiBF and
TE fibers synthesized with RM82 was consistently lower than that of those
synthesized with RM257. This can be attributed to the significantly higher
viscosity of the s-LCE i-TE fibers prepared by RM82, which suppresses the
thermal migration of ions within the system. Therefore, to minimize the influence
of physical morphology differences, such as viscosity, exhibited by s-LCE i-TE
fibers synthesized using RM82 on the thermoelectric performance, and to
ensure a valid comparison of the thermoelectric properties between m- and s-
LCE i-TE fibers, RM82 is not used for the preparation of s-LCE i-TE fibers in
this work.

Response: We sincerely appreciate your valuable feedback. The accuracy of
calculations indeed significantly impacts the computational results. In the
calculation of diffusion length mentioned in this study, the diffusion length (L)
for different systems is computed using the formula 𝐿 = √6𝐷 𝜏 based on the
𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑠

In the RM257 system, the large number of unreacted double bonds primarily
affects the overall viscosity of the system and the spatial structure of molecular
chains. These factors have already been considered and are reflected through
the diffusion coefficient and residence time of ions within the system.
In s-LCE i-TE fibers, it is precisely the differences in viscosity and
molecular chain structure compared to the main-chain system that led to
significant disparities in the diffusion coefficients and residence times of cations
and anions. These differences ultimately result in variations in the diffusion
length. Therefore, in the calculations presented in this study, the presence of
numerous unreacted double bonds in the side-chain system did not
compromise the accuracy of the computations. Instead, it serves as strong
evidence demonstrating the distinct ion diffusion behaviors between main-chain
and side-chain systems.

Point 5:
During LCE fiber preparation, how does the method ensure alignment of liquid
crystal units? While anisotropy in backbone LCE fibers is observable via POM,
the absence of POM characterization for RM257-derived side-chain LCE fibers
does not prove their liquid crystal units exhibit isotropy. Figure 1(a)’s schematic

Response: We sincerely appreciate you bringing up this issue. During the
preparation of LCE fibers, the ordered alignment of the liquid crystal mesogens
primarily originates from the injection process. To more clearly illustrate the
underlying mechanism, we have provided Supplementary Figure 1 to explain
this process. As shown in the figure below, the liquid crystal mesogens exist in
a disordered state within the syringe. However, as the syringe is compressed
and the injection proceeds, the applied shear stress gradually induces a
transition of the mesogens from a disordered to an ordered state. This
phenomenon has also been documented in the literature (Angew. Chem. 2023,
135, e202308793). The shear force generated at the nozzle during the injection
molding process is the main factor responsible for inducing the directional
alignment of the liquid crystal mesogens.
We apologize for the oversight in omitting the POM characterization of the
s-LCE i-TE fibers. Through POM testing of the s-LCE i-TE fibers prepared with
RM257 before and after solution impregnation, it is observed that when the fiber
and polarizing filter are oriented at 45°, the s-LCE i-TE fibers exhibit vibrant
multicolored patterns both before and after impregnation. In contrast, at 0°,
a completely dark scene is observed. This indicates that the s-LCE i-TE fibers
maintained monodomain alignment and anisotropic characteristics throughout
the solution impregnation process (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2023, 62,
e202214339; Adv. Sci. 2024, 11, 2400557). Based on these findings, we have
revised the schematic of the s-LCE fibers in Figure 1(a) to accurately reflect the
anisotropic orientation of the liquid crystal mesogens. Additionally, the more
disordered and tightly packed molecular chain structure of the s-LCE fibers is
primarily validated using two-dimensional wide-angle XRD of both m- and s-
LCE fibers. The results reveals that the m-LCE fiber exhibits an order parameter
and molecular spacing of 0.44 and 4.67 Å, respectively. In comparison, the s-
LCE fiber shows values of 0.31 and 4.45 Å, indicating smaller interchain
spacing and lower orientation degree. This confirms that the molecular chain
structure of the s-LCE fiber is more disordered and tightly packed compared to
the m-LCE fiber. However, the depiction of the liquid crystal mesogen alignment
in Figure 1(a) may have been exaggerated. Therefore, we have revised the
illustration to better align with the experimental findings, enhancing the
professionalism and accuracy of the figure.

manuscript, which is lower than the performance reported in our previous work
(25.8 mV K-1). This is attributed to the fact that this work adopted the
impregnation methods from the previous article (Nat Commun 2025, 16, 5445)

structures on thermopower is not considered. In fact, m- and s-LCE fibers
exhibit significant differences in raw materials and fabrication processes,
leading to substantial variations in molecular chain spatial arrangement and
system viscosity, which in turn affect the binding energy and thermal migration
rates of cations and anions. Detailed preparation methods for s-LCE fibers have
been supplemented in the manuscript. Following your suggestion, we
conducted a detailed investigation of the impregnation concentration and time

impregnation time. This improvement is attributed to the superior ordering of

interactions among the three components and is relatively sensitive to ambient
humidity. By contrast, the LCE i-TE fibers reported here leverage their intrinsic
structural advantages to promote ion thermodiffusion, and exhibit excellent
humidity resistance due to their hydrophobicity and highly crosslinked network,
thereby offering distinct advantages. Nevertheless, this paper provides an
important optimization strategy for improving the performance of
multicomponent ionic thermoelectric materials. Therefore, we have prominently
cited this important reference in the introduction. In the performance

testing protocol, while our thermopower measurements follow the approach

Beyond the presentation, I have concerns regarding the studied materials,

and then state that only one end of the mesogen was attached to the backbone.
This raises the question: where does the backbone come from in this case?
The methods section does not describe the preparation of the side-chain LCEs
at all, leaving me with the impression that the material is instead a partially
reacted main-chain structure with free-floating chains. The presented NMR
measurements also do not confirm the presence of a side-chain network, but
merely indicate unreacted sites, which is consistent with both scenarios.
Furthermore, it is not stated whether the materials were mono- or polydomain,
and the preparation section likewise provides no information on this point. The
only clue is a microscopy image of an m-LCE under crossed polarisers, which
suggests a monodomain network. This should be explicitly addressed, since
anisotropic structure affects ionic transport - a point the authors themselves
emphasise on several occasions.
Response:
Thanks for raising this question. We apologize for the oversight in not including
the fabrication process of the s-LCE i-TE fiber in the manuscript, which may
have led to the misunderstanding that it was derived from the m-LCE i-TE fiber.
In fact, the preparation method and material selection for the s-LCE fiber differ
significantly from those of the main-chain type. The s-LCE fiber was
synthesized using RM257 as the mesogen, EDDET and PETMP as the soft
segment and crosslinker, respectively, and DPA as the catalyst. Specifically, 2.4
g of RM257, 0.7 g of EDDET, and 0.1 g of PETMP were dissolved in 2.4 ml of
ethyl acetate under continuous stirring at 70 °C for 1 hour. Then, 9 μl of DPA
was added, and stirring continued for 1 minute to obtain the LCE precursor
solution. This solution was injected into a polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) tube
with an inner diameter of 2 mm and left horizontally at room temperature for 12
hours. The resulting s-LCE fiber was then peeled from the tube. The s-LCE i-
TE fiber was subsequently obtained by immersing the s-LCE fiber in an ionic
liquid solution for a specific duration using a solution immersion method. This
procedure is consistent with our group’s previously published work (Nature
Communications, (2025)16:5445) and has now been thoroughly detailed in the
materials preparation section of the revised manuscript.
Based on the synthesis route of the s-LCE fiber and previously reported
literature, the molecular backbone of the s-LCE fiber synthesized using RM257,
EDDET, and PETMP is primarily composed of poly(methyl)acrylate (Adv. Funct.
Mater. 2025, e15319), derived from the polymerizable acrylate end groups of
RM257. NMR results presented in the manuscript confirm that only one end of
the mesogenic unit is attached to the backbone in the s-LCE fiber. Furthermore,
repeated DMA measurements of the s-LCE i-TE fiber consistently show that the
storage modulus remains higher than the loss modulus in the low-frequency
region (0.1 rad/s). This indicates that the material exhibits quasi-solid gel
characteristics due to its internally stable network structure, with no liquid-like
behavior suggestive of an absence of network formation. These results confirm
the presence of a well-defined side-chain polymer network.
Additionally, through the observations of POM clearly reveal that the m-
LCE i-TE fiber exhibits colorful patterns when oriented at 45° to the polarizer,
while appearing completely dark at 0°, indicating its monodomain structure and
anisotropic nature (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2023, 62, e202214339; Adv. Sci.
2024, 11, 2400557). We apologize for not explicitly describing or emphasizing
this phenomenon in the manuscript. In fact, the monodomain and anisotropic
structure of the m-LCE i-TE fiber plays a critical role in promoting the thermally
driven migration of ions under a temperature gradient, which indicates that
liquid crystal mesogens are all uniformly aligned along the same direction,
forming nanochannels between molecular chains that are favorable for ion
migration with low migration resistance, enabling ions to achieve high-speed
thermal migration and further amplifying the thermal migration difference
between cations and anions, thereby optimizing thermoelectric performance
(Adv. Mater. 2025, 2504592; Adv. Mater. 2021, 33, 2103755). To highlight this
important feature, we have supplemented the POM section with a detailed
explanation of how the monodomain alignment and anisotropic properties
enhance ion transport, providing further insight into the underlying mechanism.

Thank you for your valuable suggestion. The strong humidity resistance of the
m-LCE i-TE fiber primarily stems from two factors (Adv. Funct. Mater. 2013, 23,

(1) The intrinsic hydrophobicity of the LCE material effectively prevents the

influence of air humidity on the internal structure of the LCE. The structural

enhanced humidity resistance.

the thermopower of the m-LCE i-TE fiber maintains over 85% of its original
performance across relative humidities ranging from 30% to 90%.

Page 13, Line 460: “Notably, the s-LCE i-TE fibre demonstrates convergence
of loss modulus toward storage modulus at higher frequencies, indicating

my earlier concerns about material preparation. Repeating the measurement
could clarify whether the material shows fatigue. Additionally, please explain

Response:
Thank you for your valuable suggestion. Following your suggestion, we have
re-evaluated the DMA performance of the s-LCE i-TE fiber. As shown in Figure
4(d), the new results differ from the initial measurements, the storage modulus
now consistently remains higher than the loss modulus across the frequency
range of 10-1 to 102 rad/s, confirming the stable quasi-solid gel characteristics
of the material and further validating the formation of a robust internal network
structure in the s-LCE i-TE fiber. To ensure reliability, the experiment is repeated
three times, and all trials support this conclusion. After consulting with the DMA
testing engineer, we identified that the previously observed convergence of
storage and loss moduli in the high-frequency region is likely due to improper
sample clamping or baseline calibration errors during the initial test. These
procedural issues introduced significant inaccuracies that did not reflect the
intrinsic properties of the material. We sincerely apologize once again for this
oversight.
Additionally, the selected frequency range (10-1 to 102 rad/s) is determined
based on both the material’s structural responsiveness within this range and
practical technical constraints of DMA measurement (Mechanics of Materials
146 (2020) 103369; Journal of Applied Polymer Science 100(1), 2006:677-683):
(1) In the low-frequency region (0.1 rad/s), the stimulus acts like a very
slow “tap” on the material. Under such conditions, polymer chains have
sufficient time to stretch, slide, and reorganize, reflecting macroscopic structural
features and long-term behavior. The fact that the storage modulus consistently
exceeds the loss modulus in this regime indicates that the material does not
flow like a liquid over extended timescales and maintains its shape due to a
stable internal network. This behavior not only confirms the formation of a
robust cross-linked structure but is also characteristic of typical gels or cross-
linked solid materials.
(2) In the high-frequency region (100 rad/s), the stimulus resembles a rapid
“impact.” The material cannot adjust globally at this pace, only local segments
respond, reflecting microstructural behavior of the material. Here, both storage
and loss moduli increase, indicating stronger resistance to fast deformation.
The polymer chains lack sufficient time to relax, leading to greater energy
storage. This frequency range primarily probes the rigidity and flexibility of chain
segments.
(3) The intermediate frequencies serve as a transition zone bridging
macroscopic and microscopic responses where the material shifts from liquid-
like to solid-like dominance. The crossover point between storage and loss
moduli in this region marks the transition between viscous and elastic behavior.
Lower frequencies were avoided to prevent excessively long test durations,
which can introduce increased measurement error and reduced accuracy. On
the other hand, higher frequencies are excluded due to the risk of amplified
inertial effects in the clamps and sensors, which could likewise compromise
measurement reliability.
The frequency range of 10-1 to 102 rad/s is selected for DMA measurement
of the LCE i-TE fiber in this study primarily because it not only confirms the
formation of a stable internal network structure but also consistently
demonstrates quasi-solid gel-like behavior across this span. Throughout the
entire frequency range, the storage modulus remains higher than the loss
modulus, indicating that the LCE i-TE fiber maintains elasticity-dominated
mechanical characteristics and verifies its elastomeric nature. Furthermore, this
range avoids technical challenges associated with extremely low or high
frequencies, ensuring that the test yields highly reliable data with good signal-
to-noise ratios within a reasonable experimental timeframe.

Response:
Thank you for your valuable suggestion. “Self-powered” refers to a device that
does not rely on external power sources (such as batteries or the grid), but
instead harvests energy from its surrounding environment and converts it into
electricity to meet all or part of its operational power needs. In this work, the
mechanism of the LCE i-TE device primarily involves the conversion of low-
grade thermal energy into electrical energy through ionic thermodiffusion.
However, it operates mainly in a capacitive mode, which differs significantly
from the working mechanism of traditional electronic thermoelectric materials.
Therefore, the term “self-powered” may not be entirely appropriate here. Based
on a review of the literature, the term “thermal-charge” is more accurate and
professional for describing ionic thermoelectric materials due to their unique
capacitive operating mode. This expression has been widely adopted in
numerous published studies and is therefore considered more suitable (Nano-
Micro Lett. (2025) 17:204).
We apologize for the insufficient detail in the manuscript regarding the
structure of the LCE device, which may have led to confusion. The device
consists of two integrated modules: a substrate module and a thermoelectric
module. The substrate module was fabricated by weaving a 2-meter m-LCE
fiber into a 3 cm × 6 cm rectangular textile using a rib-knitting technique. The
thermoelectric module was integrated into this LCE textile by embedding and
interlacing a m-LCE i-TE fiber. Silver wires serving as electrodes were similarly
embedded and connected to the cold and hot ends of the fiber. The tight woven
structure of the LCE textile ensures robust integration of the thermoelectric fiber
and silver wires. The detailed textile structure, temperature difference utilization
strategy, and physical images of the device are shown in the Figure 5(g-h) and
Figure S38-39. Meanwhile, it should be noted that the woven structure does not
affect the output voltage of the device. As illustrated in the schematic diagram
of the temperature difference utilization mechanism, the device is attached
directly to the heat source, and its output voltage is primarily influenced by the
temperature difference between the cold and hot ends, rather than by variations
in the textile weave. This observation is also supported by reports in the
literature (Nature Communications, (2025)16:5445).
Meanwhile, thank you for raising this critical issue. We acknowledge that
there is indeed a discrepancy between the descriptions and the numerical
values presented in Figure 5(i–k) and Supplementary Figure 40. This
inconsistency arose because the initial voltage of the device during testing is
not 0 V, which led to the mismatch in reported values. To address this, we have
retested the output performance of the device to ensure data accuracy and rigor.
As shown in the revised Figure 5(i–k) and Supplementary Figure 40, when the
device is attached to a beaker and exposed to alternating cold and hot water, it
generated output voltages of 270 mV and 206.6 mV under temperature
differences of 10.3 K and 7.5 K, respectively. Furthermore, when affixed to the
human arm, it produced an output voltage of 44.5 mV under a temperature
gradient of just 1.7 K.
